    You’re not alone in this moment

    A hard moment is not a failure — and you don’t have to carry it by yourself. Reach out right now, in whichever way feels possible:

    Call 988 Text 988

    The 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline — free, confidential, 24/7, anywhere in the U.S.

    Call SAMHSA: 1-800-662-4357

    SAMHSA’s National Helpline — free, confidential treatment referrals and support, 24/7.

    Grounding & prayer

    A prayer for this moment: Lord, I can’t carry this moment alone, and I don’t have to. You are my refuge and my strength, always ready to help. Slow my breathing, steady my heart, and walk me to the next right step. Amen.

    Before you stop drinking

    Alcohol withdrawal can be dangerous. If you drink heavily, don’t try to stop suddenly on your own — talk to a doctor first, or call SAMHSA at 1-800-662-4357 and ask what to do. Getting medical help to stop is not weakness; it’s wisdom.

    Gratitude Journal

    Private, for your eyes only. On hard days, this list is evidence: proof that even in the middle of the rebuilding, there is something to thank God for. Your entries are saved on this device, so they will be here when you come back.

    Nothing here yet. Your first entry can be as small as a cup of coffee, a phone call, or waking up sober this morning.

    My Next Right Step

    Recovery is built one small, honest step at a time. Don't write the whole staircase — just the next step: the call to make, the meeting to attend, the thing to hand to God today.

    THE FOUNDER'S JOURNEY

    One day at a time

    Steven Gregory — counting from August 20, 2026 (Day 0).

    Why this app exists

    My name is Steven Gregory. After 34 years of struggling with alcohol — rehabs, jail, losing everything I owned more than once, including my career — I started this recovery journey on August 20, 2026. I am living it the only way it can be lived: one day at a time.

    My Christian faith is the ground I stand on. I pray every day, and prayer is what keeps me holding on. When I say God restores, I mean it the way Joel 2:25 says it — He gives back what was lost.

    I built My Recovery Journey, and now this app, for the person who feels alone in recovery tonight. You are not alone. These are the same tools I use every day: count the days, read the reflection, write the gratitude, take the next right step.

    “One Day at a Time. One Step Toward a New Life.”

        Install My Recovery Journey

        This is your icon — the silver path through the navy evergreens to the sunrise. Once installed, it sits on your home screen and opens full-screen, just like an app from the store.

        On iPhone — Safari

        1. Open this page in Safari on your iPhone (if you're in another app's browser, tap its menu and choose “Open in Safari”).
        2. Tap the Share button — the square with an arrow pointing up ↑ — at the bottom of Safari.
        3. Scroll down the list and tap “Add to Home Screen.”
        4. Check the name reads My Recovery Journey, then tap Add in the top corner.
        5. Find the silver-path icon on your home screen and tap it — the app opens full-screen from there, every day.

        On Android — Chrome

        1. Open this page in Chrome.
        2. Tap the ⋮ menu in the top corner.
        3. Tap “Install app” or “Add to Home screen.”
        4. Tap Install / Add to confirm — the silver-path icon lands on your home screen.

        Good to know

        Installing this way is free and needs no App Store account and no password. It is the same app, with the same icon, ready each morning for your counter, reflection, and journal. The App Store version is a separate, later step — this home-screen app works today.

        The Hijacked Brain

        It is not a character flaw. Your brain was hijacked — and a hijacked brain can heal.

        If you have ever promised yourself in the morning that you were done — meant it with everything in you — and then found yourself drinking or using by evening anyway, this lesson is for you. That broken promise was probably not a lie. And it was not proof that you are weak. Something real had happened inside your brain.

        Deep in the middle of the brain sits a small survival system. Its job is to notice the things that keep you alive — food, water, rest, sleep, the people you love — and mark them: that mattered; do it again. It does the marking with a chemical messenger called dopamine. Think of dopamine less as a pleasure chemical and more as a highlighter pen. It tells the brain what to pay attention to, what to remember, and what to repeat.

        Alcohol and other addictive drugs break into that system. They trigger a rush of dopamine far beyond anything nature provides — not a little more, but many times more. Faced with a signal that loud, the brain does exactly what it was built to do: it learns, fast and deep. It starts treating the substance the way it treats food and water — as something needed to survive. That is the hijacking. The drug stops looking like one choice among many and starts feeling like a necessity. And a craving is the sound of that alarm going off.

        A brain flooded that often protects itself the only way it can: it turns the volume down. It makes less dopamine, and the receptors that receive it grow less sensitive. Two results follow, and both are familiar. You need more of the substance to feel what you used to feel — that is tolerance. And the everyday things that once registered — a good meal, a laugh, music, a clear morning — barely move the needle. Life feels flat and gray, and people mistake that flatness for their new personality. It is not a personality. It is a turned-down system.

        Here is the cruel twist researchers keep finding: over time, the liking fades while the wanting grows. Long after the substance has stopped being enjoyable, the craving can still hit like a wave — set off by a place, a person, a time of day, a hard feeling. That is why someone can honestly hate everything addiction has cost them and still feel pulled toward it. The wanting is a learned alarm. It is not a verdict on your character.

        At the same time, the front part of the brain — the prefrontal cortex, the part that weighs consequences, plans ahead, and says wait — grows quieter under addiction’s strain. So at the very moment the alarm is at its loudest, the brakes are at their softest. If you have ever felt like part of you was watching yourself do something you did not want to do, that is not an excuse. It is an honest description of a system out of balance.

        Now the part that matters most: the brain heals. A brain is not fixed wiring. It is living tissue that reshapes itself around what you repeatedly do — scientists call that neuroplasticity. Stay stopped, and the dopamine system slowly recovers. Ordinary pleasures start to register again. The brakes grow stronger. Slowly is the honest word: think months, not days, and the line does not move straight. Sleep, food, movement, meetings, prayer, the honest work of recovery — these are not just good habits. They are the daily physical therapy of a brain learning how to live again.

        So if your brain has felt like the enemy, hear this plainly: it was hijacked — and what has been hijacked can be taken back. One day, one right step, at a time.

        Try this today

        Don’t just take this on faith — watch it happen. The next time a craving shows up today, don’t wrestle it head-on. Open the 5-4-3-2-1 grounding exercise, work through it slowly, and then notice the urge itself: it rises, it levels off, and it starts to fall — usually inside twenty minutes. That is the hijacked alarm running out of breath. Every craving you ride out is one more rep in retraining your brain.

        King Baby

        The part of us that still wants its own way — and the freedom that comes from seeing it clearly.

        King Baby is a name for a pattern many people in recovery recognize in themselves: the inner demand that life, people, and even God should arrange themselves around what we want, when we want it. It might say, “I want what I want, now.” When life answers slowly — or says no — the response can be anger, sulking, scheming, or shutting down. The body may be grown. In that moment, the feelings are very young.

        This is not an insult to aim at somebody else, and it is not a label that sums up a person. King Baby names a part that can stir in any of us. A toddler expects the room to revolve around hunger, tiredness, and desire because a toddler has not yet learned anything else. Trouble comes when that old expectation keeps quietly making adult decisions: in traffic, at work, in a meeting, in a marriage, or in recovery itself.

        The name became familiar through Tom Cunningham’s 1986 Hazelden pamphlet, King Baby. Cunningham drew on older recovery writing, including psychiatrist Harry Tiebout’s phrase “His Majesty, the Baby.” The idea belongs to recovery-community wisdom, not to a medical textbook. It is not a clinical diagnosis, and it does not appear in the DSM. That honesty matters. The phrase is useful because it gives us language for a pattern we can observe and change — not because it explains everything about us.

        How does the pattern show itself? We may expect limits and instructions to bend because our case feels special. We may need praise to feel secure, while an honest correction lands like rejection. Feelings can swing between extremes: a plan is wonderful until it disappoints us, and then it seems worthless. Authority can be a sore spot; we might argue, tune it out, or try to get one person to overrule another. Underneath can sit a frightened, ashamed child who worries about being left out, found lacking, or no longer in control.

        That frightened child helps explain the demanding surface, but does not excuse the harm it can do. King Baby can spend money the family needs, demand attention while someone else is hurting, punish loved ones with silence, or walk away from help because help came with conditions. Recovery asks us to tell the truth about both sides: the fear is real, and so is our responsibility to choose a better response and make amends when we miss the mark.

        Left unnamed, the pattern can run recovery from the back seat. We may want the benefits of the program without its patience. A sponsor who disagrees feels like an enemy. A meeting seems useless unless it moves us. Other people are expected to change first. Resentment grows because reality will not obey, and isolation can follow. Naming the pattern does not magically remove it, but it creates a pause. In that pause, we can ask what we actually need, what fear is speaking, and what the next right step is.

        Recovery teaches grown-up answers: surrender instead of control, honesty instead of performance, patience instead of demand, and service instead of keeping score. Surrender does not mean becoming passive. It means accepting that our will is not the center of the universe. Honesty lets us state a need plainly instead of manipulating for it. Patience makes room for other people and for God’s timing. Service turns the gaze outward: Who can I encourage? What useful thing can I do that nobody may notice?

        Most of us will not retire this pattern in a single day. We learn to spot it sooner. We hear the inner voice rising — now, mine, unfair — and we do not have to obey it. We can breathe, call someone, pray, wait, or accept a limit without making others pay for our disappointment. We do not shame the frightened child within us. We simply stop handing that child the keys. One honest pause at a time, we grow into the people recovery is making us.

        Try this today

        In today’s journal, watch for one moment when King Baby wanted to drive. It might be small: a delay, a correction, a closed door, or attention going to someone else. Finish two sentences: “King Baby wanted…” and “The grown-up response was…” If no moment has happened yet, use a recent one. Let the page be honest, not punishing — noticing the pattern is the practice.
